answer.rationale:
The strongest signal here is temporal: a release went out 2 hours ago and write-path p99 has been climbing for 90 minutes, which fits a release-induced regression better than a capacity or regional story. Removing the suspected cause is the only intervention that addresses etiology rather than symptoms; add_capacity, failover, and read-replica routing all leave a bad build in the write path, and route_read_replicas is close to irrelevant since the pain is on writes, not read contention on the primary. Circuit breaking would shed exactly the settlement writes we are told not to lose.

I am spending the single verification on memory_b1 because it is the memory my chosen action leans on hardest, and its summary is suspiciously clean: 'rollback finished without customer impact' says nothing about the traffic conditions at the time. If that day-18 rollback happened in a quiet window with a small delta to the prior build, it is weak evidence for rolling back at daily settlement peak with heavy in-flight writes. I want the original record for the write volume at the time, whether writes were drained or in-flight requests were dropped, and how far the prior build was behind schema-wise. A rollback across a migration boundary during peak writes is a way to lose customer writes, which is the one thing the objective forbids. memory_b6 supports the mechanism (canary cohorts surfaced a regression within an hour) and is why I want this staged rather than global.

So: guarded scale. Revert on a small cohort of write traffic first, watch p99 on that cohort against the rest, and only widen if the divergence confirms the release as cause. This keeps the blast radius small if the release is innocent and the real driver is peak-load saturation, in which case the honest next-window move is capacity (memory_b3) and I will have gathered the evidence to justify it. The competing hypotheses stay live: release regression, peak-load saturation, or an unrelated dependency slowdown that merely coincides with the deploy. All six inherited memories describe successes, which means I am reasoning from a record with no visible failures and should not treat any of them as a general rule.
